_comment: Source of truth for the export's two theme palettes. brand/apply_brand.py is
the ONLY writer — it rewrites the `light:`/`dark:` literals inside the
`const themes = {` block of every exported page, which the export's own
renderer then emits as CSS custom properties (--canvas, --ink, --accent, ...)
on its root div. Every key below becomes one CSS variable of the same name.
Direction: the corporate B2B register of idnow.io — a near-black canvas with
a blue cast, a single hot coral-orange accent, flat surfaces, white ink.
Replaces the design tool's warm cream + coral, which read as a personal
portfolio rather than as an engineering vendor.
The values are taken from the reference site's own published theme palette
(canvas #02060A, accent #FB5E31, surface #0F1317, borders #35383B), not from
a description of it. An earlier pass of this file guessed 'teal' from a prose
summary and shipped a palette that missed the target completely — the accent
is the one token worth reading off the source rather than inferring.
CONTRAST IS LOAD-BEARING. Every pair below clears WCAG AA (4.5:1); the
numbers in _measured are computed, not estimated, and
tests/test_hero_contrast.py enforces the hero's composited floor separately.
Two traps, both already paid for once:
* A WHITE label on the orange accent is 3.11:1 and FAILS. The label is
near-black in both themes (6.53:1). Dark-on-hot is also what makes the
button read as a brand mark rather than as a warning.
* The dark accent #FB5E31 is only 2.89:1 on a light canvas. The light theme
therefore uses the darkened #B23C0A, chosen so it clears 4.5 on the
DARKEST light surface (#e8e8e8, 4.84:1) and not merely on white — the
obvious #C2410C passes on white and fails at 4.23:1 on that surface.
_inverseBtn_comment: The export's secondary CTA — a solid button that sits ON the accent band and
on the About page, where an accent-filled button would vanish. The export
ships it as warm cream with a warm ink label, both left over from the old
palette. This is the cool equivalent: white surface, near-black label.
_fonts_comment: The export routes ALL typography through two JS expressions in its own
script — `fontDisplay` (41 headings) and `fontBody` — each a one-line
`ar ? <arabic> : <latin>` ternary. Rewriting those two lines is far more
Only the LATIN arm is ours to set. The arabic arm stays Amiri / Noto Sans
Arabic: Plus Jakarta Sans has no arabic subset, and substituting a face that
cannot render the script would break the ar locale outright.
Single-family by design. The export shipped a serif display (editorial) and
the repo's hero layer had pushed every heading to JetBrains Mono (technical);
both read as a different product than the corporate B2B target, which is one
geometric sans throughout. Plus Jakarta Sans is vendored as a variable woff2
in seo/vendor/fonts/, so all weights cost one request.
_hardcoded_comment: Chrome the export paints with LITERAL hex instead of theme variables, so the
palette rewrite above cannot reach it: the auth modal (panel, inputs, borders,
helper text), the mobile nav panel wordmark, and the seo:footer link strip.
These are intentionally dark in BOTH themes, like the footer.
Left alone they stay warm brown-grey on a near-black site — the single most
visible way this palette swap could look half-finished.
Keys are the export's OLD warm values; values are the new equivalents, role
for role. This map assumes it runs against a PRISTINE export: it translates
warm -> new, so re-pointing it at a site/ this layer already transformed
would find none of its keys. Rebuild site/ from the export (or from a
socialGrey is called out separately because this layer WRITES it (social
marks are muted so the accent stays scarce). It must equal the mapping target
for the old grey below — otherwise the simpleicons rewrite would flip it back
on every run and the layer would never reach a fixed point.
